question: What is the main benefit of using a topical medication?

options.A: It completely bypasses the need for patient consent.
options.B: It minimizes systemic side effects by acting locally.
options.C: It guarantees complete absorption into the bloodstream.
options.D: It works faster than intravenous injections every time.

explanation: Topical medications are applied right where they are needed. This keeps most of the drug out of the general circulation and prevents unwanted body-wide reactions. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for a midwife to know that the skin is a selective barrier?

options.A: It proves that all skin creams work instantly.
options.B: It dictates how well a drug can penetrate the tissues.
options.C: It means medications can never cross the outer layer.
options.D: It shows that skin absorbs every chemical equally.

explanation: Because the skin is built to keep things out, the type of cream or ointment used determines how much medicine actually gets absorbed into the body. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which layer of the skin is the main barrier against drug absorption?
explanation: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer made of dead, protective cells. It blocks most foreign substances and chemicals from easily entering the body. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why do medicines applied to the vagina absorb much faster than those put on regular skin?

options.A: Mucous membranes produce oils that dissolve all types of drug molecules.
options.B: Vaginal mucous membranes lack a tough stratum corneum and have rich blood supplies.
options.C: Vaginal tissues are always warmer than the external skin surface.
options.D: The skin on the body has a thicker layer of fat underneath it.

explanation: Without a tough outer layer, and with a rich network of blood vessels nearby, topical treatments can enter the bloodstream very quickly through mucous membranes. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which topical preparation is a greasy, oil-based formula that helps trap moisture?
explanation: Ointments have a high oil content. This creates a heavy barrier that stops moisture from escaping the skin surface. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the main difference between a cream and an ointment?

options.A: Creams are water-and-oil emulsions that wash off easily, whereas ointments are greasy and oil-based.
options.B: Creams are only used for systemic drug delivery through transdermal patches.
options.C: Creams contain alcohol to dry out weeping wounds while ointments add moisture.
options.D: Creams are solid blocks meant to melt at body temperature inside body cavities.

explanation: Creams mix water and oil together, meaning they wash off easily and do not leave a heavy, greasy feel like pure ointments do. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the main reason for putting barrier cream on a newborn's bottom?

options.A: To deliver antibiotics directly into the baby's bloodstream
options.B: To lower the infant's body temperature during a fever
options.C: To shield the skin from moisture and irritating stool enzymes
options.D: To cure systemic bacterial infections spreading from the gut

explanation: Barrier creams create a protective layer over the skin, keeping urine and stool from breaking down delicate baby skin. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal use for topical medications in midwifery?

options.B: Treating severe maternal hypertension with a skin cream
options.C: Protecting infant skin from diaper rash

explanation: Severe high blood pressure needs systemic medications taken by mouth or through an IV, not a local skin cream. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why should a midwife use a clean spatula instead of fingers to take ointment from a shared jar?

options.A: To prevent introducing bacteria into the container
options.B: To follow hospital rules on saving money on gloves
options.C: To make sure the exact dose is measured in grams
options.D: To prevent the ointment from absorbing into skin

explanation: Using bare or even gloved fingers directly in a jar can spread germs into the product, which might cause an infection later. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the correct way to apply a medicated cream to a mother's skin?

options.A: In a thin, even layer using gentle strokes following the direction of hair growth
options.B: By piling a thick mound over the lesion and covering it with heavy tape
options.C: By spraying it quickly from a distance without touching the patient
options.D: By rubbing it forcefully in circles until the skin turns bright red

explanation: Gentle strokes following hair growth prevent skin irritation and help spread the medication evenly without blocking hair follicles. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why is it important to clean off old cream before applying a fresh dose?

options.A: To punish the patient for not cleaning themselves earlier in the day
options.B: To make the medication tube last longer between clinic visits
options.C: To prevent buildup and ensure proper contact between the new drug and clean skin
options.D: To ensure the hospital records match the pharmacy stock count

explanation: Old layers of cream can block fresh medicine from reaching the skin and can trap dirt or bacteria underneath. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is getting informed consent especially important when applying topical treatments in midwifery?

options.A: Topical drugs are always dangerous and require signed court documents.
options.B: Many applications involve sensitive areas like the perineum or breasts where privacy and dignity matter greatly.
options.C: Patients have the legal right to manufacture their own herbal creams at home.
options.D: Midwives cannot touch a patient's skin without a medical doctor present.

explanation: Treating intimate areas requires clear communication and respect for the woman's body to help her feel comfortable and maintain trust. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is a common sign of a mild allergic reaction to a topical cream?

options.A: Complete numbness of the entire left arm and hand
options.B: Yellowing of the whites of the eyes within minutes
options.C: Sudden redness, itching, and burning at the application site
options.D: Immediate drop in the patient's blood pressure and pulse

explanation: A local skin reaction usually shows up right where the cream was applied, causing irritation, a rash, or itching. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h7)

question: What should a midwife do first if a mother develops a bad rash after using a prescribed cream?

options.A: Stop the medication, wash the area gently with water, and report the reaction.
options.B: Tell the mother to ignore it until her next scheduled clinic appointment next month.
options.C: Scrub the affected skin vigorously with harsh antiseptic soap and alcohol.
options.D: Apply a thicker layer of the same ointment to cover the new rash completely.

explanation: Washing the area stops further exposure to the drug, and reporting the reaction ensures the patient gets a safer alternative. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which details must be written down when documenting a topical medication?

options.A: The cost of the tube of cream purchased from the pharmacy
options.B: Date, time, drug name, concentration, and application site
options.C: The brand of soap the patient used to bathe that morning
options.D: The personal phone number of the attending obstetrician

explanation: Good clinical records need precise details showing what drug was given, when it was applied, and exactly where it went on the body. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h8)

question: Why is checking back on a patient after applying a topical treatment important?

options.A: To confirm whether the treatment achieved its goal and check for adverse skin reactions
options.B: To ensure the patient throws away the empty tube of cream immediately
options.C: To collect data for a research paper on chemical manufacturing
options.D: To prove to hospital management that the midwife worked a full shift

explanation: Checking on the patient later lets the midwife see if the cream is helping or if it is causing any skin irritation that needs attention. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h8)
